content: The use of lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assays has been evaluated for diagnosing active tuberculosis (TB) in individuals living with HIV, particularly those with advanced disease or low CD4 cell counts. The diagnostic accuracy of LF-LAM varies depending on the clinical setting and patient population. For HIV-positive adults with TB symptoms, the sensitivity and specificity of LF-LAM in inpatient settings are 52% and 87%, respectively, while in outpatient settings, sensitivity drops to 29% with a specificity of 96%. When used in all settings, the sensitivity is 42% and specificity is 91%. For HIV-positive adults without regard to TB symptoms, LF-LAM demonstrates a sensitivity of 62% and specificity of 84% in inpatient settings, and a sensitivity of 31% with specificity of 95% in outpatient settings. Among individuals with advanced HIV disease (CD4 ≤ 200), the sensitivity and specificity of LF-LAM in inpatient settings are 64% and 82%, respectively, while in outpatient settings, sensitivity is 21% and specificity is 96%. For those with CD4 ≤ 100, sensitivity in inpatient settings is 57% and specificity is 90%, while in outpatient settings, sensitivity is 40% and specificity is 87%. In children living with HIV, data on LF-LAM are limited, but sensitivity ranges from 42% to 56% and specificity from 80% to 95%, depending on the study and setting. The test is particularly useful in populations where TB diagnosis is challenging, as it relies on urine samples rather than sputum, making it safer and easier to collect. However, challenges such as stock-outs, limited shelf life, and delays in treatment initiation remain. Economic evaluations suggest that LF-LAM could be cost-effective, especially among hospitalized HIV-positive adults in high TB/HIV burden settings. Qualitative studies highlight its ease of use, rapid turnaround time, and minimal infrastructure requirements, though operational challenges must be addressed to optimize its implementation. The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends LF-LAM for diagnosing active TB in HIV-positive inpatients with advanced disease, serious illness, or CD4 counts <200, regardless of symptoms. For outpatients, it is conditionally recommended for those with CD4 counts <100. The 2019 WHO guidelines expanded the scope of LF-LAM use to include all symptomatic or seriously ill inpatients and outpatients with advanced HIV disease. Research priorities include developing more accurate LAM-based tests, evaluating LF-LAM in children and asymptomatic individuals, and studying its integration into routine HIV care. Additionally, cost-effectiveness and user perspectives on LF-LAM implementation require further investigation.
